slides.title: The loop: how a model writes an answer
slides.summary: The model predicts one token, adds it to the text, and runs again on the longer text. It stops when its best guess is the end token.
body: Give the model “The pizza is ready” and ask what comes next. Each run of the model does the same job: turn the text into vectors, pass them through the transformer's layers, and score every possible next token. The second figure below shows one run in full.

ul: Run 1 reads “The pizza is ready” and picks “ for”.
Append it. The input is now “The pizza is ready for”, one token longer.
Run 2 reads all of that, including the word it just wrote, and picks “ you”. Then “!”, one token per run.

body: <mark>The model never writes a whole answer at once. Every token comes from a full run over everything so far, including the tokens it has already written.</mark>

body.h: How does it know it's finished?

body: It doesn't decide in any deep sense. Every answer in its training data ended with a special end token, so once a reply looks complete, that token becomes the most likely prediction. When it wins, the loop stops.

ul: The end token wins: the usual way a reply ends.
A length limit: the app caps the number of tokens, which can cut a reply off mid-sentence.
A stop sequence: the app can also stop when a chosen piece of text appears.

body.text: Inside every run, attention lets the newest token look back at everything before it. That's what makes the model's guesses fit the context, and it's the subject of the next chapter.

body.more: Isn't re-reading the whole text every run slow?
body.text: It would be. Models keep the work already done for earlier tokens in a KV cache, so each run only has to compute the newest token.
body.link: The KV cache in Output & inference

body.more: What does the end token look like?
body.text: It's one of the tokenizer's special tokens, such as <|endoftext|> in GPT-2. Chat models use an end-of-turn token from their chat template.

steps.caption: The model gets the token IDs of the text so far.

item.label: The pizza is ready for
item.sub: run 1 read 4 tokens and picked “ for” (42%)

steps.caption: The winner is appended. The input is now one token longer.

item.label: The pizza is ready for you
item.sub: run 2 read 5 tokens and picked “ you” (58%)

steps.caption: The model runs again on everything, including its own last word.

item.label: The pizza is ready for you!

steps.caption: One token per run, every time.

item.label: end token
item.sub: run 4: the reply looks complete, so the end token wins (81%)

steps.caption: The end token is never shown. It just tells the app to stop the loop.

figure.alt: The generation loop for "The pizza is ready". Run 1 reads The, pizza, is, ready and predicts " for" at 42%; it is appended. Run 2 reads the five tokens and predicts " you" at 58%; appended. Run 3 reads six tokens and predicts "!" at 47%; appended. Run 4 reads "The pizza is ready for you!" and predicts the special end token at 81%, so the loop stops and the reply is finished. Finishing is just one more prediction: answers in training ended with an end token, so the model learns to predict it once a reply is complete. Apps also stop at a length limit. Probabilities are illustrative.
figure.caption: Each run's winner joins the input for the next run. The reply ends when the end token wins.

figure.alt: How an LLM predicts the next token for "The pizza is ready". 1: split into tokens The, space pizza, space is, space ready. 2: look up token IDs, 791, 23317, 374 and 5644 in GPT-4. 3: turn IDs into vectors of numbers, plus position. 4: run the transformer: N identical layers, each with layer norm, self-attention, where ready looks back at every earlier token, layer norm and a feed-forward network; then layer norm and linear plus softmax, giving one score per vocabulary token. Self-attention is the subject of the next chapter. 5: score every possible token, for 42%, to 31%, at 12%, now 6%, and pick one, giving The pizza is ready for. 6: add it to the text and run again, one token at a time. Values are illustrative.

slides.title: GPT: Generative Pre-trained Transformer
body: GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer.

ul: A transformer is a type of neural network architecture designed to process sequences of information using attention.
It was introduced in the 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need”.
Before transformers, sequence models commonly used architectures such as RNNs and LSTMs, which processed text more sequentially.

body: In 2017, Google researchers published “Attention Is All You Need”. Their transformer reads all the tokens at once, and attention links any two words directly, however far apart they are.

items.label: 2017 “Attention Is All You Need”
items.sub: the transformer is introduced, for translation

items.label: 2018 GPT-1
items.sub: OpenAI pre-trains a transformer on books

items.label: 2020 GPT-3
items.sub: learns tasks from a few examples in the prompt

items.label: 2022 ChatGPT
items.sub: a GPT model fine-tuned for conversation

viz.html: Numbers are parameters, the model's learned weights.

slides.title: Why transformers need attention
slides.summary: A word's meaning depends on the words around it. Attention lets each word look at the others and decide which ones matter.
body: For every word, attention answers one question: which other words should I focus on right now, and how much?

ul: “The cat sat on the mat, because it was tired.” Here “it” is the cat.
“…because it was cozy.” Now “it” is the mat.
“…because it was cold weather.” Now “it” is the weather.

body: Self-attention means attention between tokens of the same text: each token looks at the other tokens around it and works out how they relate.
<mark>Without attention, a word looks the same wherever it appears. With it, the surrounding words decide what it means.</mark>

ul: I went to the bank to deposit money. → a place for money
I sat on the bank of the river. → the side of a river

body.text: Each token makes a query, a key and a value, scores every pair and blends the values by those scores. The Attention chapter walks through it step by step.

figure.alt: Attention lets a word look at the other words in its sentence; thicker lines mean more attention. In "The cat sat on the mat, because it was tired", "it" attends most to "cat" (0.71), so it means the cat. With "cozy", "it" attends most to "mat" (0.66). With "cold weather", "it" attends most to "weather" (0.58). In "I went to the bank to deposit money", "bank" attends to "money" and "deposit": a place for money. In "I sat on the bank of the river", "bank" attends to "river": the side of a river. Weights are illustrative.
figure.caption: The highlighted word decides what “it” and “bank” mean. Attention is how the model finds that word.

slides.title: Token + position: building the model's input
slides.summary: Each token gets two vectors: one for what the word is, one for where it sits. Add them, stack the results, and you have the matrix the transformer reads.
body: Before the transformer can do anything, every token has to become a list of numbers. That takes two lookups and one addition.

body.h: Step by step, for “The cat sat”

ul: 1 · Token IDs. The tokenizer turns the text into numbers, for example The → 791, cat → 8415, sat → 7731.
2 · Token embedding: what. Each ID picks its row from the token table, which holds one learned vector per word in the vocabulary. “cat” always gets the same row.
3 · Position embedding: where. Each slot picks a row from the position table: one vector for position 0, one for position 1, and so on. “cat” sits in position 1, so it gets row 1.
4 · Add. Add the two vectors number by number: first plus first, second plus second. The result has the same length.

body.note: How the adding works: a position vector always has the same length as a token vector: the model's width. Line the two up and add slot by slot: 1st + 1st, 2nd + 2nd, and so on. In GPT-2 both have 768 numbers, so the input has 768 too. Its position table has 1,024 rows, one per position, which is why GPT-2 can read at most 1,024 tokens.

body: <mark>The transformer never sees the word and its position separately. It gets one vector per token that carries both.</mark>

body.note: Like a place card at a wedding: one card with the guest's name and their table number. Same guest, different table, different card.

body.h: The input is now a matrix

body: Stack the three sums on top of each other, one row per token, and you get a grid of numbers: a matrix. Here it has 3 rows (tokens) and 4 columns (numbers per token), so its shape is [3, 4].

ul: Rows grow with the text. A 1,000-token prompt makes 1,000 rows.
Columns are fixed by the model. GPT-2 uses 768 numbers per token; Llama 3 8B uses 4,096.

body: <mark>This matrix is the whole input. The transformer reads all its rows at once, and every layer passes on a matrix of the same shape.</mark>

body.more: Why add them instead of putting them side by side?
body.text: Joining the two vectors end to end would double their length and make every layer bigger and slower. Adding keeps the size the same. With hundreds or thousands of numbers per vector there's room for both kinds of information, and training learns to keep them apart.

body.note: Is this RoPE? No. Adding a position vector is how GPT-2 worked. Most modern models use RoPE instead, covered on the next slide.

body.more: Why does word order need this at all?
body.text: Without position, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” give the model the same three vectors.

viz.html: One row per token, one column per number: shape [3, 4]. Values are illustrative.

figure.alt: For “The cat sat”, each token looks up its token embedding (what the word is) and its position embedding (where it sits), and the two are added number by number. For cat in position 1: [0.2, −0.4, 0.7, 0.1] + [0.1, 0.3, −0.2, 0.4] = [0.3, −0.1, 0.5, 0.5]. The three input vectors are stacked into a 3 by 4 input matrix that goes into transformer layer 1. Below: cat in position 1 and cat in position 5 give different input vectors. Values are illustrative.
figure.caption: Two lookups and one addition per token, then the rows are stacked into the input matrix.

slides.title: RoPE: how modern models add position
slides.summary: Instead of adding a position vector, RoPE turns each token's vector by an angle that depends on its position.
body: Most modern models, including Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and DeepSeek, don't add a position vector at the input. They use RoPE, short for rotary position embedding.

ul: Picture a token's vector as an arrow.
Position 0: no turn. Position 1: turn a little. Position 2: turn twice as much, and so on.
The arrow keeps its length, so the meaning is kept. Only its direction changes, and that shows where the word sits.

body: <mark>When attention compares two words, what matters is the angle between them. That angle depends only on how far apart they are.</mark>

Take “The cat sat” from the last slide: The is position 0, cat is 1, sat is 2. cat and sat are one step apart. If the same words appear again at positions 101 and 102 in a long story, they're still one step apart, so they get the same angle.

body.note: Two friends on a merry-go-round: wherever the ride turns, the angle between them stays the same.

body.text: Inside attention, in every layer, on the query and key vectors that attention uses to compare tokens. The token's own vector is never changed. Attention, the next chapter, explains queries and keys.
RoPE tells the model “three tokens back”, not “token 1,207”. That suits language, where nearby words usually matter most. It's also one reason context windows can be made longer after training.

body.more: Why do the pairs turn at different speeds?
body.text: Fast pairs make nearby positions look clearly different. Slow pairs change gradually over long distances. Together they tell the model how far apart words are, both close up and across a long text.
For a closer look at how models encode position, from the original fixed patterns to RoPE, read Understanding positional embeddings, by Sebastian Raschka.

cells.text: how far apart two words are
capped by the table (1,024 in GPT-2)

viz.html: A worked example: “cat” at position 1 in “The cat sat”. Only the direction changes. Values are illustrative.

figure.alt: RoPE turns each token by an angle that depends on its position. The word cat, drawn as an arrow, is not turned at position 0, turned 35 degrees at position 1, 70 at position 2 and 105 at position 3. Its length, the meaning, stays the same. Below, for “The cat sat”: cat at position 1 and sat at position 2 are 35 degrees apart, and the same words later in a long story, at 101 and 102, are also 35 degrees apart. Same gap, same angle, wherever the words are. Angles are illustrative.
figure.caption: Turn by position: the angle between two words shows how far apart they are.

slides.title: The whole transformer, in one picture
slides.summary: Text goes in, one block repeats many times, and out comes a probability for every possible next token.
body: Every GPT-style model, from GPT-2 to today's chatbots, follows this plan. Use this slide as a map: click any part on the right to jump to where it's explained.
<mark>Almost all the work happens in the transformer block, repeated many times. Bigger models mostly stack more blocks and make each one wider.</mark>
GPT-2 stacks 12 blocks, 768 numbers wide. Llama 3 8B stacks 32 blocks, 4,096 wide.

slides.title: Layer normalization: keeping the numbers steady
slides.summary: Before each main step, every token's vector is rescaled to a standard range, so the numbers don't grow too big or shrink too small as they pass through many layers.
body: The input matrix passes through dozens of layers, and each layer adds to its numbers. Left alone, they drift: some grow huge, others shrink towards zero, and training becomes unstable.

body.h: What it does to one token

ul: 1 · Subtract the average of the token's numbers, so they're centred on 0.
2 · Divide by the spread, how far the numbers typically sit from the average, so they have a standard size.
3 · Scale and shift with numbers learned in training, so the model can still pick the best range for each slot.

body: <mark class="info">In short: each number becomes “how many spreads it sits from the average”. Every token keeps its pattern but comes out the same size.</mark>
<mark>Each token is normalized on its own, using only its own numbers. However big or small it comes in, it goes out in the same steady range.</mark>

body.note: Why it matters: normalization keeps the neural network's internal representations well behaved, which makes training deep networks more stable.
Like auto-fix on a photo: too dark or too bright, it comes out looking normal. The picture itself doesn't change.

viz.html: Try ten times bigger, [60, −20, 100, 20]: the average is 40, the spread 44.7, and the result is exactly the same. Values are illustrative.

blocks.html: The spread is the standard deviation: roughly, how far the numbers typically sit from their average. For “cat” [6, −2, 10, 2]:

1 · Average: (6 − 2 + 10 + 2) ÷ 4 = 4.
2 · Distance of each number from the average: [2, −6, 6, −2].
3 · Square them, so negatives don't cancel positives: [4, 36, 36, 4].
4 · Average the squares: 80 ÷ 4 = 20.
5 · Square root, to undo the squaring: √20 ≈ 4.47.
A small spread means the numbers are bunched together; a large one means they're scattered. Dividing by it gives every token a spread of 1.
Mostly no. A vector's meaning is in its pattern, which numbers are high and which are low, and normalization keeps that exactly. It only removes the overall size.

The original Transformer and GPT-2 use LayerNorm, as shown here. Most modern models, including Llama, Mistral and Qwen, use RMSNorm, which skips step 1 and only divides by the typical size of the numbers. It's slightly cheaper and works just as well.

items.label: Read more: Normalisation, in The transformer block →

figure.alt: Where layer normalization sits: input matrix, norm, attention, norm, feed-forward; that layer is repeated N times (12 in GPT-2, 32 in Llama 3 8B); then a final norm, then predict the next token.

Layer normalization for one token. “cat” going in is [6, −2, 10, 2], average 4 and spread 4.47. The same token times 10 is [60, −20, 100, 20], average 40 and spread 44.7. LayerNorm subtracts the average and divides by the spread, and both come out as [0.45, −1.34, 1.34, −0.45], average 0 and spread 1: the pattern is kept, only the size changes. Values are illustrative.
figure.caption: Same pattern, steady size: big or small going in, the same range comes out.

figure.alt: Two tokens drawn as lines on a 2D plot, slot n1 to n4 across, value up. Before: the bunched token [3.5, 4.5, 3.8, 4.2] has average 4 and spread 0.38, so its line looks almost flat and its shaded strip, one spread either side of the average, is thin. “cat” [6, −2, 10, 2] also has average 4 but spread 4.47: a big zigzag with a wide strip. After layer norm: bunched becomes [−1.31, 1.31, −0.53, 0.53] and “cat” becomes [0.45, −1.34, 1.34, −0.45]. Both have average 0 and both strips run from −1 to 1. Each line keeps its own zigzag shape; only the size is standardised.
figure.caption: A small spread means the numbers are bunched together; a large one means they're scattered. Dividing by it gives every token a spread of 1.

slides.title: Multi-head causal self-attention
slides.summary: The attention step in every layer of a GPT-style model. Each part of the name says one thing about how it works.
body: Self-attention is how a token works out what it means from the other words in the same text. A word on its own is often unclear: in “The cat sat on the mat because it…”, “it” could be the cat or the mat. So “it” looks back over the sentence, scores how relevant each word is, and takes in the most from the best match, “cat”.

body.h: What each part of the name means

ul: Self-attention: each token looks at the other tokens in the same text to work out what it means. “it” looks back and finds “cat”.
Causal: a token can look only at itself and earlier tokens, never later ones. The model writes one token at a time, so later words don't exist yet.
Multi-head: several attention heads run side by side, each looking for something different. Their results are combined into one new vector.

body: <mark>Each token comes out with a new vector that mixes in what it found in the earlier words, gathered by many heads at once.</mark>

body.note: Like a few readers going over the same sentence, each with a different question, who then pool their notes.

text: GPT-2 has 12 heads in each of its 12 layers; Llama 3 8B has 32 in each of its 32 layers.
<mark>Nobody tells a head what to look for: each one learns its job during training.</mark>

body.more: Why can't a token look ahead?
text: Because the model learns by guessing the next word. In training it sees a whole sentence at once and practises at every position together: after “The cat sat” it should guess “on”; after “The cat sat on”, “the”; and so on.

<mark>If “sat” could look ahead, the answer “on” would be right there to copy. The model would score perfectly in training and learn nothing. And when it writes for real, the next word doesn't exist yet. The mask hides every later word, so each position has to actually predict.</mark>

body.text: Each head turns every token into a query, a key and a value, scores every pair, and mixes the values. The next chapter walks through it step by step.

figure.alt: Multi-head causal self-attention for “it” in “The cat sat on the mat because it”. The next words, “was tired”, are not written yet and are masked, so “it” can't look at them. Head 1 points back to “cat” (who “it” refers to), head 2 to “mat” (the place), and head 3 to “because” (the word just before). The three results are combined into a new vector for “it” that carries the cat, on the mat, and the words around it. Real models use 12 to 100+ heads per layer and learn what each one looks for.
figure.caption: Look back only, ask several questions at once, combine the answers.

figure.alt: Attention heads drawn as a 3D stack of sheets, one behind another. The same input, 5 tokens (The cat sat on the) by 768 numbers, feeds every sheet at once. Each sheet is one head with its own look-back grid, where later words are masked: head 1 links back to “cat”, head 2 looks at the previous word, head 3 at the first word, head 4 at itself, head 5 spreads its attention, and head 6 looks two words back; the stack continues to head 12. All heads' outputs are joined (12 × 64 = 768) and mixed into an output of 5 by 768. Numbers from GPT-2.
figure.caption: The heads are a stack, not a queue: every one reads the same input at the same moment, and their outputs are joined and mixed.

slides.title: Feed-forward: each token, on its own
slides.summary: After attention gathers context, a small network processes each token's vector by itself.
body: Attention lets tokens share information. The feed-forward layer (also called the MLP, short for multi-layer perceptron) then works on each token on its own, using what it just gathered.

ul: 1 · Expand: stretch the vector 4× wider, from 768 to 3,072 numbers in GPT-2.
2 · Keep the strong signals: a simple curve (GELU) lets strong signals through and turns the rest down.
3 · Shrink: squeeze back to 768 numbers and add the result to the token's vector.

body: <mark>Attention moves information between tokens. Feed-forward works on each token by itself. Every layer does both.</mark>

body.note: About two-thirds of a model's parameters are in these layers, and research suggests much of what it knows, like facts, is stored here.
Attention is the group discussion; feed-forward is each person thinking it over alone.

body.text: The wider middle gives room to detect thousands of patterns at once: each middle number acts like a detector for something, such as a topic, a grammar rule or a fact. Shrinking back keeps the vector the same size for the next layer.
body.link: The MLP in depth, in The transformer block

body.text: Llama and most new models use SwiGLU, a version with a gate that decides how much of each signal to let through. Mixture-of-experts models keep many feed-forward networks and send each token to just a few of them.

figure.alt: The feed-forward layer for the token “it”. Its 768 numbers fan out into 3,072 detectors, four times wider, each checking for one meaning. For “it”, the detectors for a pronoun, refers to an animal, one thing (singular) and subject of a verb fire. Others, such as about food, past tense, a place and a number, come out negative and are switched to 0. Only the detectors that fired feed the shrink step, which squeezes them back into 768 numbers: an update meaning an animal, one thing, the subject, which is added to “it”'s vector. The same network runs on every token at once. Sizes from GPT-2; detector names and values are illustrative.
figure.caption: Expand to give room for thousands of meanings, keep the ones that fire, shrink them back into one update.

slides.title: Residual connections: add, don't replace
slides.summary: Each step adds its output to the vector instead of replacing it.
body: After attention, the transformer doesn't replace a token's vector. It adds attention's output to it. The input “skips” around the step, so this is called a skip or residual connection.
<mark>Each step adds an update. Nothing the token already knew is thrown away.</mark>
This is called a residual update: the layer adds a small change instead of replacing the vector, which is why we say it nudges.

ul: Nothing is lost: meaning and position stay in the vector all the way up.
Deep models can train: learning flows back easily through the additions.

body: Every layer has two: one around attention, one around the feed-forward step.

body.more: How does this fit with layer normalization?
body.text: The norm tidies a copy going into each step. The step's result is then added back onto the untouched original.

viz.html: Output = input + update. Values are illustrative.

figure.alt: Residual connections inside a transformer block, repeated N times. On the left, the diagram: x goes through layer norm and multi-head attention while a green residual line copies x around them and adds it back at a plus sign; then layer norm and feed-forward, with a second residual line and plus sign; the output goes to the next block. On the right, the same block as numbers, following “it”: x in is [1, 2, 3], and a residual copy is kept. Layer norm turns a copy into [−1.22, 0, 1.22]; attention gives an update [0.2, −0.5, 0.7]. At the plus sign, [1, 2, 3] + [0.2, −0.5, 0.7] = [1.2, 1.5, 3.7]. A residual copy of that is kept; layer norm turns a copy into [−0.84, −0.57, 1.41]; feed-forward gives an update [0.1, 0.3, −0.2]. At the second plus sign, [1.2, 1.5, 3.7] + [0.1, 0.3, −0.2] = [1.3, 1.8, 3.5]: x out. x only changes at the plus signs; the norms work on copies, so x keeps its full values. Updates are illustrative.
figure.caption: Inside every transformer block: two residual lines copy the input around each step and add it back.

slides.title: Transformer layer, in motion
slides.summary: Watch “it” go through one transformer layer: attention looks back, the MLP refines, and each result is added back.

ul: 1 · Input: each token is a column of 768 numbers.
2 · Self-attention: “it” scores every earlier word, softmax turns the scores into weights, and “it” takes a weighted mix of them, mostly “cat”. 12 heads do this at once.
3 · MLP: each token, on its own, fans out into 3,072 detectors (768 → 3,072). Some fire, the rest switch off, and the firing ones shrink back into 768 numbers.
4 · Out: the same shape as the input. GPT-2 stacks 12 of these layers.

body: <mark>Attention lets tokens share information; the MLP then works on each token alone. Both add their result back to the main line.</mark>

figure.alt: An animation of one transformer layer, GPT-2 sizes, on “The cat sat on the mat because it”, following “it”. 1, input: 8 tokens become 8 columns of 768 numbers, the input matrix. 2, multi-head causal self-attention: “it” looks back at every earlier word, never ahead; its query is compared with each word’s key, and softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to 1: cat 0.62, mat 0.14, because 0.07, it 0.05, sat 0.04, The 0.03, the 0.03, on 0.02. The new “it” is a weighted mix, mostly “cat”. 12 heads do this in parallel, 64 numbers each, joined back into 768, and the result is added to the main line. 3, MLP, drawn as an hourglass: “it”’s 768 numbers fan out into 3,072 detectors, 4 times wider; some fire and are kept, the rest stay off and are set to 0; only the firing ones feed back into 768 numbers, an update that is added back again. 4, out: 8 tokens by 768 numbers, the same shape; “it” now carries “the cat”. GPT-2 repeats this layer 12 times.
figure.caption: The animation loops every 22 seconds. Weights are illustrative.

slides.title: Many layers, many heads, one KV cache each
slides.summary: Every layer runs many attention heads, and keeps a cache of past keys and values so each new token only does its own work.
body: Each attention head turns every token into three vectors: a Q (query: what am I looking for?), a K (key: what do I offer?) and a V (value: what do I pass on?). The new token compares its Q with every K and takes in the matching Vs.

ul: Past tokens don't change. A token can't look ahead, so the K and V of “cat” come out the same on every run.
So every layer saves them in its own KV cache: a K and a V for each earlier token, for every head.
Each new token does only its own work: it computes its Q, K and V, saves its K and V, and reuses everyone else's.

body: <mark>Thanks to the cache, each run after the first works on just one new token, which is why answers can stream out quickly.</mark>

body.note: Q isn't cached: only the newest token is asking, and it asks once.

body.text: Memory. It grows with every token, in every layer. The table shows GPT-2's numbers; big models with long texts can need gigabytes, more than the model itself.
body.link: The KV cache, in Output & inference

figure.alt: An LLM as a stack of identical transformer layers, layer 1 up to layer N (12 in GPT-2). The tokens “The cat sat on the” enter at the bottom. Inside every layer, multi-head attention runs heads 1 to 12 side by side, each making its own Q, K and V, then a feed-forward network works on each token alone. Beside every layer is its own KV cache: a K row and a V row for every earlier token. The new token saves its K and V into the cache and reuses the stored ones; Q isn't cached. At the top, linear and softmax pick the next token, “mat”. Values are illustrative.
figure.caption: Many layers, many heads per layer, and a KV cache for each layer so past tokens are never worked out again.

slides.title: Linear & softmax: from a vector to the next token
slides.summary: After the last layer, the final token's vector becomes a score for every word in the vocabulary, and softmax turns the scores into probabilities.
body: Only the last token's vector is used to predict what comes next. For “The cat sat”, that's “sat”: 768 numbers that, after all the layers, carry the whole sentence.

ul: Linear: compare the vector with every word in the vocabulary, one dot product each. GPT-2 gets 50,257 scores, called logits. A high score means “this word fits next”.
Softmax: turn the scores into probabilities that add up to 100%. A bigger score gets a much bigger share.

body: <mark>The model doesn't choose a word here. It gives every word a probability; a separate sampling step picks one.</mark>

viz.html: For “The cat sat”. Each 1-point drop in score cuts the share by about 2.7×. Values are illustrative.

blocks.html: Raise e (about 2.72) to the power of each score, then divide each by the total. The results are always positive and add up to 1.

One column of 768 numbers per vocabulary word. A word's score is how well its column lines up with the last token's vector. GPT-2 reuses its token embedding table here, so each word's input and output vectors are the same; many newer models learn a separate table.
A sampling step picks one token from these probabilities, shaped by settings like temperature and top-p. The token is appended and the whole model runs again.

figure.alt: The output head of a GPT-style model, for “The cat sat” with GPT-2 sizes. 1: only the last token, “sat”, is used: its 768 numbers after the final norm. 2: a linear layer, a table of 768 by 50,257 numbers, takes one dot product per vocabulary word. 3: the result is 50,257 scores, called logits, for example on 6.0, down 4.9, in 4.0, there 3.3, and banana −2.1. 4: softmax turns the scores into shares of 100%. 5: probabilities: on 61%, down 20%, in 8%, there 4%, all others together 7%, banana 0.02%. Next, a sampling step picks one token, usually a likely one such as “on”; it is appended, giving “The cat sat on”, and the whole model runs again. Values are illustrative.
